slides.title: Sentences do different jobs
slides.text:
Some sentences **tell** something.
The sun is hot.

Some sentences **ask** something.
Is the sun hot?

Some sentences **tell you to do** something.
Drink some water.

slides.title: Telling and asking
slides.text:
A **telling** sentence gives a fact. It ends with a full stop.
My cat is black.

An **asking** sentence is a question. It ends with **?**
Where is my cat?

slides.title: Commands
slides.text:
A **command** tells someone what to do. It often **starts with the verb**.

**Sit** down.
**Close** the door.
**Please wash** your hands.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Read each sentence.
2. Ask: does it **tell**, **ask**, or tell me **to do** something?
3. Look at how it starts and ends.

Commands start with an action word. Questions end with **?**

example.explain:
**Cut** and **Squeeze** start the sentences. They tell you what to do, so they are **commands**.

'It tastes great!' tells something. It is not a command.

together.passage: It is time to plant a seed. Fill a cup with soil. Put the seed in the soil. Water it every day. Soon a green leaf will grow.
options: It is time to plant a seed.
Soon a green leaf will grow.
Put the seed in the soil.
together.hint: Which sentence tells you what to do? Look for one that starts with an action word.
together.good: Yes! **Put** is an action word at the start. It tells you what to do.

sentences: It is time to plant a seed.
Fill a cup with soil.
Put the seed in the soil.
Water it every day.
Soon a green leaf will grow.
evidence.stem: The answer was: Put the seed in the soil. Tap 2 OTHER sentences that are commands.
evidence.wrong: This sentence tells you something. It does not tell you to do something.

checks.passage: Do you like dates? I like them a lot. Try one now!
checks.why: It ends with a question mark and asks what you like.

checks.passage: Look at the sky. The moon is full tonight. Can you see it?
checks.why: It tells us something about the moon. It does not ask or tell us to do anything.

checks.passage: Please line up at the door.
options: It tells someone to do something.
checks.why: **Please line up** tells the class what to do. It is a command.

again.title: Three hats
again.text:
Imagine three hats.

The **teller** hat: gives facts.
The **asker** hat: asks questions.
The **boss** hat: gives commands.
again.example:
'Open your book.' → boss hat
'Is it open?' → asker hat
'The book is open.' → teller hat

slides.title: Verb mood
slides.text:
The **mood** of a verb shows the writer's **purpose**.

**Indicative**: states a fact or opinion.
The bus leaves at seven.

**Interrogative**: asks a question.
Does the bus leave at seven?

slides.title: Imperative mood
slides.text:
The **imperative** gives a command, a request or advice. The subject **you** is hidden.

**Bring** your lunch.
**Please be** on time.
**Let's go** together.

slides.title: Why it matters
slides.text:
Writers choose the mood that fits the job.

A story mostly uses the **indicative**.
Instructions use the **imperative**.
An interview uses the **interrogative**.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Read the sentence and ask what it **does**.
2. Check the clues: a verb at the start? A question mark? A plain fact?
3. Find other sentences in the text with the same purpose.

The sentences that do the same job are your proof.

sentences.t: The school trip is on Monday.
Bring a hat and a water bottle.
Please return the form by Thursday.

example.explain:
Sentences 2 and 4 give instructions with the hidden subject **you**. They are **imperative**.

Sentence 1 states a fact (indicative). Sentence 3 asks (interrogative).

together.passage: Our class is holding a book swap next week. Every student can bring up to three books. Please write your name inside each book. Choose books that are in good condition. Do you have a book you have read many times? Someone else might love it too!
together.stem: What is the mood of the sentence 'Please write your name inside each book.'?
options: indicative, because it states a fact
interrogative, because it asks a question
imperative, because it gives an instruction
imperative, because it ends with a full stop
together.hint: Who is being told to do something? What is the hidden subject?
together.good: Yes! It tells students what to do, with the hidden subject **you**. It is **imperative**.

sentences: Our class is holding a book swap next week.
Every student can bring up to three books.
Please write your name inside each book.
Choose books that are in good condition.
Do you have a book you have read many times?
Someone else might love it too!
evidence.stem: The answer was: imperative. Tap the OTHER sentence in the imperative mood.
evidence.wrong: This sentence states a fact or asks a question. Find the other instruction.

checks.passage: How many planets are in our solar system?
checks.stem: What is the mood of this sentence?
checks.why: It asks a question, so it is **interrogative**.

checks.passage: Turn off the lights when you leave the room.
checks.stem: What is the mood of this sentence?
checks.why: It gives an instruction to **you**, so it is **imperative**.

checks.passage: Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level.
checks.stem: What is the mood of this sentence?
checks.why: It states a fact, so it is **indicative**.

again.title: What is the job?
again.text:
Ask one question: **What is this sentence trying to do?**

Tell me a fact → indicative
Ask me something → interrogative
Get me to act → imperative
again.example: 'Pass me the salt.' → It wants me to act → **imperative**.

slides.title: The conditional mood
slides.text:
The **conditional** mood talks about what **would**, **could** or **might** happen.

I **would** help you if I had time.
We **could** win if we practise.

slides.title: Imagining the unreal
slides.text:
To imagine something that is **not true now**, use **if + past verb**, then **would + verb**.

If I **had** a camel, I **would ride** it to school.
(I do not have a camel.)

slides.title: Real or imagined?
slides.text:
Real and possible: **If** it **rains**, we **will stay** inside.

Imagined: **If** it **rained** here every day, the desert **would be** green.

The verb forms show the difference.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Decide: is the writer talking about something **real** or **imagined**?
2. Look for **would**, **could** or **might**.
3. Find other sentences in the passage with the same pattern: if + past verb, would + verb.

sentences.t: If our town had a beach, we would swim every weekend.
We could also learn to sail.

example.explain:
Sentence 1 shows the beach is **not real**. So sentence 2 uses **had** and **would swim** to imagine it.

**could learn** continues the imagined idea.

together.passage: Our class wrote about an imaginary invention. Noor wrote about a robot that cleans classrooms. If every school had one, teachers would save a lot of time. The robot could also water the plants. If it ___ to talk, it might even help students with spelling.
together.hint: The robot is imaginary. What verb form comes after 'if' when you imagine something?
together.good: Yes! To imagine something unreal, we use **if + past verb**: if it **learned**, it **might** help.

sentences: Our class wrote about an imaginary invention.
Noor wrote about a robot that cleans classrooms.
If every school had one, teachers would save a lot of time.
The robot could also water the plants.
If it ___ to talk, it might even help students with spelling.
evidence.stem: The answer was: learned. Tap 2 OTHER sentences in the conditional mood.
evidence.wrong: This sentence states a fact about the class or Noor. Find sentences with would, could or might.

checks.passage: If I ___ a bird, I would fly over the mountains.
checks.why: The writer is not a bird, so this is imagined: **if I were**, then **would fly**.

checks.passage: If you heat ice, it melts.
checks.stem: Is this sentence real or imagined?
options: real, because it is a fact that always happens
checks.why: Heating ice really does melt it. This is a fact, so it uses present verbs, not would.

checks.passage: If we had more time, we ___ visit the old souq.
checks.why: **had** shows an imagined situation, so the result uses **would**.

again.title: Dreams use would
again.text:
When you **dream** about something that is not true:

Part 1: if + past verb
Part 2: would / could / might + verb
again.example:
I am not rich. → If I **were** rich, I **would build** a library.

We do not live by the sea. → If we **lived** by the sea, we **could fish**.

slides.title: The subjunctive mood
slides.text:
The **subjunctive** expresses wishes, demands and situations contrary to fact.

Wishes and unreal ideas use **were** for every subject:
I wish I **were** taller.
If she **were** here, she would know.

slides.title: Demands and suggestions
slides.text:
After verbs like **insist, suggest, recommend, demand** and phrases like **it is important that**, use the **base verb**, with no -s.

The doctor recommended that he **rest**.
It is essential that every student **be** on time.

slides.title: Avoid mood shifts
slides.text:
Do not switch moods without a reason in one sentence.

Shift: **Open** your book, and **you should read** page ten.
Consistent: **Open** your book and **read** page ten.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Look for trigger words: **wish**, **if** (unreal), **insist**, **suggest**, **recommend**, **it is important that**.
2. After them, use **were** or the **base verb**.
3. Find other sentences in the passage that follow the same pattern.

sentences.t: The coach wishes the season were longer.
He suggests that each player stretch before training.

example.explain:
**wishes … were**: a wish about something unreal.
**suggests that each player stretch**: base verb, no -s.

'Training starts at five' is a plain fact, so it is indicative.

together.passage: Before the school trip to the Asir mountains, our teacher held a short meeting. She insisted that every student ___ a warm jacket, because the evenings can be cold. She also recommended that each of us carry a small torch. One boy joked that he wished he were a mountain goat, so he would not need boots. The teacher laughed and said that the trip would begin at six in the morning.
together.hint: Look at the trigger word **insisted that**. What form of the verb follows it?
together.good: Yes! After **insisted that**, we use the base verb: **every student bring**.

sentences: Before the school trip to the Asir mountains, our teacher held a short meeting.
She insisted that every student ___ a warm jacket, because the evenings can be cold.
She also recommended that each of us carry a small torch.
One boy joked that he wished he were a mountain goat, so he would not need boots.
The teacher laughed and said that the trip would begin at six in the morning.
evidence.stem: The answer was: bring. Tap 2 OTHER sentences in the subjunctive mood.
evidence.wrong: This sentence states a fact or reports what happened. Find sentences with a wish or a recommendation.

checks.passage: It is important that the baby ___ enough sleep.
checks.why: After **it is important that**, use the base verb: **get**.

checks.passage: If I ___ the principal, I would add a longer break.
checks.why: This is unreal (the writer is not the principal), so the subjunctive uses **were**.

checks.passage: First, mix the flour and water, and then you should knead the dough.
checks.stem: How should the sentence be fixed to avoid a shift in mood?
options: First, mix the flour and water, and then knead the dough.
First, you mixed the flour and water, and then knead the dough.
First, mix the flour and water, and then you kneaded the dough.
First, would you mix the flour and water, and then knead the dough.
checks.why: **mix** is imperative, so the second instruction should be imperative too: **knead**.

again.title: Spot the trigger
again.text:
Some words switch the verb into a special form.

**wish / if (unreal)** → **were**
**insist / suggest / recommend / it is important that** → **base verb**
again.example:
The teacher suggests that Ali (reads / read) more.

Trigger: **suggests that** → base verb → **read**.
